title: Glory on the Mountain, Need in the Valley
summary: On a high mountain Jesus is transfigured before Peter, James, and John; Moses and Elijah appear with him, and a voice from a bright cloud declares him the Father's beloved Son and commands the disciples to listen to him. Coming down, Jesus identifies John the Baptist as the promised Elijah, heals a boy with seizures whom the disciples could not help, and teaches them about faith the size of a mustard seed. He predicts his death a second time, and in Capernaum he provides the temple tax for himself and Peter through a coin found in a fish's mouth.
story:
Six days after Peter's confession and Jesus' first prediction of his death, three disciples see his glory. The order matters. Jesus has just said that the road to his kingdom runs through suffering and has promised that some standing there would see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom (16:28); now the Father confirms that the one who must suffer is his beloved Son, and the three see a preview of his glory. The chapter then descends from the mountain into a valley of failure and need: a suffering boy, disciples with too little faith, a second passion prediction that grieves them. The glory is real, but it does not remove the cross.

The closing story about the temple tax, found only in Matthew, returns to the theme of sonship with which the chapter began. On the mountain the Father calls Jesus ‘My beloved Son’; in Capernaum Jesus says that the sons of the king are free. The Son of the one whose house the temple is has no debt to it, yet he pays so as not to give offense, a small act of humility that anticipates how he will give his life. The question of how Jesus relates to the temple and its institutions will grow sharper in Jerusalem (21:12-17; 24:1-2), and the chapter's final words prepare for the teaching on offense and care for the little ones that fills chapter 18.
historical:
Matthew does not name the mountain, and the question has been debated since antiquity. The identification with Mount Tabor, the isolated dome that rises about 575 meters above the Jezreel Valley in lower Galilee, is attributed to Origen in the third century, and Cyril of Jerusalem names Tabor in his Catechetical Lectures (12.16, around 350); Byzantine and Crusader churches were built on its summit, and the present Franciscan church there was completed in 1924. Many modern scholars favor Mount Hermon, the high massif (about 2,800 meters) above Caesarea Philippi, where chapter 16 was set; others suggest Mount Meron in upper Galilee. Matthew says only that it was a high mountain and that they were by themselves. The parallels are Mark 9:2-29 and Luke 9:28-43, and 2 Peter 1:16-18 recalls hearing the voice ‘on the holy mountain’.

The scribes' teaching that Elijah must come first (verse 10) rests on Malachi 4:5-6 (Malachi 3:23-24 in the Hebrew Bible), the last words of the prophetic books in the Christian Old Testament. Ben Sira, around 180 BC, says Elijah is ready at the appointed time to turn the heart of the father to the son and restore the tribes of Jacob (Sirach 48:10), and the Mishnah preserves later debate about what Elijah will do when he comes (m. Eduyot 8:7). Jesus affirms the expectation and says it has been met in John the Baptist, whom Herod Antipas imprisoned and beheaded (14:1-12). Matthew alone adds that the disciples understood he meant John (verse 13), completing what Jesus had said in 11:14.

The two-drachma tax of verse 24 was the annual temple tax. Exodus 30:11-16 required every man counted in the census to give half a shekel ‘to atone for your lives’, and after the exile the community pledged a third of a shekel yearly (Nehemiah 10:32). By the first century the half-shekel was paid every year by Jewish men from twenty years old, in Judea and throughout the Diaspora. The Mishnah says the collection was announced on the first of Adar and that the changers' tables were set up in the provinces on the fifteenth and in the temple on the twenty-fifth (m. Shekalim 1:1-3), and it had to be paid in the silver coinage of Tyre (m. Bekhorot 8:7; t. Ketubbot 13:20). Philo describes the sacred money gathered in city after city and carried to Jerusalem by chosen envoys (Special Laws 1.76-78); Josephus says Babylonian Jews stored their half-shekels at Nehardea and Nisibis until they could be escorted to Jerusalem (Antiquities 18.312); and Cicero's speech For Flaccus (59 BC) defends a Roman governor of Asia who in 62 BC had seized the Jews' temple gold at Apamea and Laodicea (For Flaccus 28.67-69). Not everyone agreed the tax was owed. One Qumran text rules that the half-shekel is to be given only once in a lifetime (4Q159, Ordinances, fragment 1 2:6-7), and the Mishnah records that Ben Bukhri testified that a priest who paid did not sin, implying priests were exempt, while Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai insisted a priest who did not pay did sin (m. Shekalim 1:4).

After the temple was destroyed in AD 70, Vespasian ordered every Jew, wherever he lived, to pay the same two drachmas each year to the temple of Jupiter Capitolinus in Rome (Josephus, Jewish War 7.218; Cassius Dio 66.7.2). This fiscus Judaicus, as it was called, was also charged on women and on children from the age of three, as tax receipts on potsherds from Edfu in Egypt show. Under Domitian it was collected harshly; Suetonius remembered seeing, as a young man, a man of ninety examined in court to see whether he was circumcised (Domitian 12.2). Nerva, who succeeded Domitian in 96, issued coins whose legend announced that the malicious prosecution connected with the Jewish tax had been removed (FISCI IVDAICI CALVMNIA SVBLATA). If Matthew wrote after 70, as most scholars think, his first readers would have heard this story while paying the same sum to a pagan temple; if he wrote before 70, as others hold, it addressed Jewish Christians still paying the temple itself.
cultural:
Moses and Elijah were the great figures of Israel's law and prophets. Both met God on a mountain, Sinai or Horeb (Exodus 24; 1 Kings 19), both ended their lives in ways later tradition surrounded with mystery (Deuteronomy 34:5-6; 2 Kings 2:11), and Malachi 4:4-5 names them together at the close of the prophets. Peter's offer of three shelters (skēnai, tents or booths) recalls the Feast of Tabernacles, when Israelites lived in booths to remember God's care in the wilderness (Leviticus 23:42-43), a feast the prophets tied to the day when the nations would come to worship the King (Zechariah 14:16). The same word, skēnē, is used in the Greek Old Testament for the tabernacle, the tent of God's presence. A bright cloud recalls the cloud of God's glory that covered Sinai and filled the tabernacle (Exodus 24:15-16; 40:34-35). The disciples' falling face down in terror, Jesus' touch, and his words ‘Get up’ and ‘Do not be afraid’ (verses 6 and 7, found only in Matthew) echo the visions of Daniel, who fell on his face, was touched by a heavenly figure, and was told not to fear (Daniel 10:9-12). Matthew calls the event a vision (horama, verse 9), a word used of God-given sights (Acts 7:31; 10:3), without suggesting it was unreal.

The father says his son is moonstruck (selēniazetai, verse 15; the only other use in the New Testament is 4:24), the popular term for seizures, which were thought to follow the phases of the moon. The Hippocratic treatise On the Sacred Disease, from about the late fifth century BC, had already argued that epilepsy has natural causes like other diseases. Matthew also says a demon was rebuked and came out (verse 18). Mustard seed was proverbial for smallness (13:31-32), and moving a mountain was a figure for doing the impossible, as Paul uses it (1 Corinthians 13:2).

The temple tax scene assumes the practice of ancient kings, who took customs duties (telē) and a poll tax (kēnsos, from the Latin census; compare 22:17-19) from subject peoples, not from their own households. The coin of verse 27 is a statēr, a four-drachma silver coin; the Tyrian shekel, a tetradrachm struck at Tyre with the head of the city's god Melqart on one side and an eagle on the other, was the coin normally used, and one of them paid the half-shekel for two men. The Sea of Galilee has several native fish. The cichlid now sold to pilgrims as Saint Peter's fish (musht) feeds on plankton and is caught in nets; Mendel Nun, a fisherman and scholar of the lake at Kibbutz Ein Gev, argued that a fish taken with a baited hook, as in verse 27, was more likely a barbel, a predator and bottom feeder that fishermen have long caught that way.
literary:
The chapter falls into four scenes. The transfiguration (verses 1 to 8) is told with deliberate echoes of Moses on Sinai: a high mountain, a period of six days (Exodus 24:16), three named companions (Exodus 24:1, 9), a cloud, a voice, and a shining face. Matthew strengthens the echo beyond Mark: only he says Jesus' face “shone like the sun” (compare Exodus 34:29-35), calls the cloud bright, names Moses before Elijah, and adds to the Father's words “in whom I am well pleased,” so that they match the voice at the baptism exactly (3:17). Dale Allison (The New Moses: A Matthean Typology, 1993) argued that Matthew consistently presents Jesus as a new Moses, and the transfiguration is one of his chief examples.

The conversation on the way down (verses 9 to 13) joins glory and suffering: as they did to Elijah whatever they wished, so the Son of Man will suffer at their hands. The healing (verses 14 to 20) contrasts mountain and valley, much as Moses came down from Sinai to find Israel in disarray (Exodus 32). Matthew tells it in seven verses where Mark uses sixteen (Mark 9:14-29), leaving out the father's cry ‘I believe; help my unbelief’ and focusing on the disciples' failure and Jesus' diagnosis. Jesus' lament, ‘O unbelieving and perverse generation’, echoes Moses' words about Israel in Deuteronomy 32:5 and 32:20. The second passion prediction (verses 22 and 23) is the shortest of the three (16:21; 20:17-19), and where Mark says the disciples did not understand (Mark 9:32), Matthew says they were deeply grieved: they understood enough to be sorrowful.

The temple tax (verses 24 to 27) is one of the few stories found only in Matthew, and it is shaped as a teaching scene rather than a miracle story. Jesus anticipates Peter before he speaks, asks a question, draws a principle from Peter's answer, and gives a command; Matthew never narrates the catch. The chapter is framed by sonship: the Father's ‘This is My beloved Son’ (verse 5) and Jesus' ‘Then the sons are exempt’ (verse 26). And the last word, ‘so that we may not offend them’ (verse 27), uses skandalizō, the verb that dominates the next chapter's warning against causing little ones to stumble.

outline.t: A boy healed; the power of faith
The second prediction of death and resurrection
The temple tax and the coin in the fish

doctrines.note: On the mountain Jesus' face shines like the sun and his clothes become as white as the light (verse 2). Unlike Moses, whose face reflected God's glory after speaking with him, Jesus is the source of the light, and the church has read the scene as a brief unveiling of the glory that belongs to him and will be seen when the Son of Man comes (16:27; 25:31).

As at the baptism (3:16-17), the Father speaks from heaven of the Son, and the cloud of God's presence overshadows them. The church has seen here a revelation of the Father's love for the Son and of the Son's divine glory veiled in his humanity, and Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologiae III.45.4) read the whole Trinity as present: the Father in the voice, the Son in his humanity, the Spirit in the bright cloud.

The disciples fail to heal the boy ‘because you have so little faith’ (verse 20). Jesus does not say they need more technique or more faith of their own, but that even faith the size of a mustard seed can move mountains, because what matters is not the size of faith but the God on whom it rests.

Jesus forbids the three to tell the vision ‘until the Son of Man has been raised from the dead’ (verse 9), and in verses 22 and 23 he predicts that he will be killed and on the third day raised to life. The glory seen on the mountain is understood rightly only in light of the cross and the empty tomb.

In the tax scene Jesus speaks as the Son of the King whose house the temple is (compare 12:6, ‘something greater than the temple is here’), and so free of its tax. He pays it anyway to avoid giving offense. After AD 70, when the tax went to Jupiter's temple in Rome, Matthew's readers would learn from this that freedom as God's children can be exercised through costly humility.

words.note: Metamorphoō, to be transformed or changed in form; four times in the New Testament (Matthew 17:2; Mark 9:2; Romans 12:2; 2 Corinthians 3:18). BDAG describes it as a change into another form. In the Gospels it names the change in Jesus' appearance; Paul uses it for believers being transformed by the renewing of the mind and into the Lord's image. The passive in verse 2 (‘He was transfigured’) suggests that God is the one who reveals him so. Matthew explains the change by the face and clothes; the word does not by itself carry a theory of how glory shone.

Agapētos, beloved; about sixty-one times in the New Testament, three in Matthew (3:17; 12:18; 17:5). In the Greek Old Testament it translates the Hebrew for ‘only’ in Genesis 22:2, 12, and 16, where Isaac is Abraham's beloved, only son whom he is asked to offer, and Matthew 12:18 uses it in quoting Isaiah 42:1 of the servant. The word ties Jesus' sonship to both the servant's calling and the path of sacrifice.

Apokathistēmi, to restore, re-establish; eight times in the New Testament. In the Greek of Malachi 4:6 (3:23), God's messenger will restore the hearts of fathers to sons, and Jesus uses the verb in verse 11, ‘he will restore all things’. The disciples later ask the risen Jesus whether he will now restore the kingdom to Israel (Acts 1:6), and Peter speaks of ‘the restoration of all things’ with the related noun (Acts 3:21). Jesus affirms the promise and says it has begun in John, who was rejected as he himself will be.

Oligopistia, littleness of faith; only here in the New Testament. It is the noun from Matthew's favorite word for the disciples, oligopistos, ‘of little faith’ (6:30; 8:26; 14:31; 16:8). Many later manuscripts read apistia, ‘unbelief’, which the King James Version follows. Jesus' diagnosis is not that the disciples have no faith, but that their trust is too small for the need, and he immediately says that even the smallest faith rightly placed is enough.

Sinapi, mustard; five times in the New Testament (Matthew 13:31; 17:20; Mark 4:31; Luke 13:19; 17:6). The black mustard of Galilee has a seed about a millimeter across that grows into a large annual shrub, and ‘as small as a mustard seed’ was a proverbial phrase. In 13:31-32 the seed pictures the kingdom's small beginning; here it pictures the smallest real faith, which is enough because God does the moving.

Didrachmon, a two-drachma piece; only here in the New Testament (verse 24 twice). The drachma was a Greek silver coin roughly equal to the Roman denarius, a day's wage for a laborer (20:2), and two drachmas equaled the half-shekel of Exodus 30:13. The word had become the everyday name for the temple tax, and after AD 70 it named the tax Rome diverted to Jupiter Capitolinus.

Statēr, a silver coin worth four drachmas; only here in the New Testament. In practice the coin was usually a Tyrian shekel, the tetradrachm required for temple payments, and one of them paid the tax for two men. Jesus' words ‘for My tax and yours’ put Peter alongside himself: the Son pays for another son of the kingdom.

Skandalizō, to cause to stumble, to trip up, to give offense; about twenty-nine times in the New Testament, fourteen in Matthew. The noun skandalon meant the trigger of a trap. Jesus pays the tax ‘so that we may not offend them’ (verse 27), not to spare himself but to keep an unnecessary obstacle out of others' way. The same verb opens the next chapter's warnings about causing little ones to stumble (18:6-9).

christ:
On the mountain Jesus is revealed as the beloved Son whose glory, usually veiled, belongs to him. The Father's words gather three Old Testament threads: the king whom God calls his Son (Psalm 2:7), the servant in whom God delights (Isaiah 42:1, which Matthew quotes at 12:18), and the prophet like Moses of whom Moses said, “You must listen to him” (Deuteronomy 18:15). Moses and Elijah, representing the Law and the Prophets and both men who met God on a mountain, speak with him and then disappear, and the disciples see ‘no one except Jesus’ (verse 8). The Law and the Prophets point to him (5:17; 11:13), and he is the one to be heard, more than a prophet. The Moses echoes are strongest in Matthew, but the text itself makes the difference plain: Moses' face shone with a reflected glory that faded (Exodus 34:29-35; 2 Corinthians 3:7), while Jesus' face shines like the sun.

The glory points forward. Jesus forbids the three to speak of the vision until the Son of Man has been raised (verse 9), so the scene is a preview of the resurrection and of the Son of Man's coming in his Father's glory promised in 16:27-28. On the way down he names the path to that glory: as the forerunner suffered, so will he (verse 12). In the valley the Son revealed in glory rebukes a demon and heals a boy his disciples could not help, showing that his authority is exercised in mercy toward the suffering, and he says a second time that he will be delivered, killed, and raised on the third day (verses 22 and 23).

The temple tax scene shows Christ's identity in a quieter key. He speaks as the Son of the King whose house the temple is, and so free from its tax; yet he pays it, and pays for Peter too. John Chrysostom (Homily 58 on Matthew) noted that the tax went back to the ransom of the firstborn and saw in Jesus' payment a condescension to others' weakness rather than a debt. Exodus calls the half-shekel ‘a ransom for his life’ (Exodus 30:12), and Matthew will later say that the Son of Man came ‘to give His life as a ransom for many’ (20:28); the link between the two ransoms is thematic rather than stated by Matthew, but it fits the chapter's pattern of a Son who is free and yet gives himself for others. His freedom exercised in humility is the pattern of the cross.
interpretation:
Jewish tradition kept the expectation that frames the middle of this chapter. The Mishnah's teachers debated what Elijah would do when he came (m. Eduyot 8:7), and the custom of setting a cup for Elijah and opening the door at the Passover meal, which developed in the Middle Ages, keeps the hope alive in Jewish homes. The temple tax, remembered in the Mishnah's tractate Shekalim, is still recalled on the Sabbath of Shekalim before the month of Adar, when Exodus 30:11-16 is read in the synagogue.

The fathers read the transfiguration as a revelation of Christ's divinity and a preparation for the cross. Origen (Commentary on Matthew, book 12, in the 240s) taught that Jesus appears differently to people according to their capacity, and that those who climb with him see him in glory. John Chrysostom (Homily 56 on Matthew, around 390) read Jesus' promise that some would not taste death as fulfilled six days later on the mountain, and in Homily 58 treated the coin in the fish as a sign both of Jesus' freedom and of his care not to offend. Leo the Great, preaching on this chapter on the Saturday before the Second Sunday of Lent in 445 (Sermon 51), said the vision was given chiefly to remove the scandal of the cross from the disciples' hearts and to show the church the glory its members would share. The apse mosaic of Saint Catherine's Monastery at Sinai, made between about 550 and 565, is among the oldest surviving images of the scene. In the fourteenth century the light of Tabor became the center of the hesychast controversy: Gregory Palamas (Triads, around 1338) argued that the disciples saw the uncreated light of God's energies, and councils at Constantinople in 1341, 1347, and 1351 upheld him. In the West the feast of August 6 was made universal by Pope Callixtus III in 1457, after news of the relief of Belgrade from the Ottoman siege reached Rome on August 6, 1456.

Modern study has asked what kind of event the transfiguration was and what the tax scene meant. Rudolf Bultmann proposed that the transfiguration was a resurrection appearance moved back into Jesus' ministry, and Robert Stein (Journal of Biblical Literature, 1976) answered that its form differs from every resurrection account. Dale Allison (The New Moses, 1993) traced Matthew's Moses typology through the scene. On the tax, William Horbury (‘The Temple Tax’, in Jesus and the Politics of His Day, edited by Ernst Bammel and C. F. D. Moule, 1984) set the story against the first-century debates over who owed the half-shekel, while Richard Cassidy (Catholic Biblical Quarterly, 1979) argued that Matthew applies Jesus' principle to civil taxes, as Matthew's readers after 70 would have experienced the Jewish tax. Rationalist interpreters of the early nineteenth century looked for a natural core to the fish story, and David Friedrich Strauss (The Life of Jesus, 1835) treated it as legend; the hard questions below take this up.

In art, Raphael's Transfiguration (1516 to 1520), finished after his death by his pupil Giulio Romano and now in the Vatican Pinacoteca, sets Christ rising in light above the mountain and, below, the disciples failing to heal the convulsed boy, holding both halves of the chapter in one canvas. Masaccio's fresco The Tribute Money (about 1425) in the Brancacci Chapel of Santa Maria del Carmine in Florence paints the tax scene as a continuous narrative: the collector's demand, Peter drawing the coin from the fish at the lakeside, and Peter paying. In the Revised Common Lectionary, Matthew 17:1-9 is read on Transfiguration Sunday in Year A, and the Roman lectionary reads it on the Second Sunday of Lent in Year A and on the Feast of the Transfiguration in Year A. In the Orthodox calendar the feast of August 6 is one of the Twelve Great Feasts.
text:
Verse 21, ‘But this kind does not go out except by prayer and fasting’, is missing from the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus, from Codex Vaticanus, and from other early Greek, Latin, Syriac, and Coptic witnesses. It appears in most later manuscripts and in the King James Version, and editors judge that copyists added it from Mark 9:29 (where ‘and fasting’ is itself a later addition). The BSB, like most modern versions, leaves the verse number empty and gives the words in a note, which is why the numbering skips from 20 to 22.

In verse 20 the earliest manuscripts read oligopistia, ‘little faith’, while many later ones read apistia, ‘unbelief’, which the King James Version translates (‘Because of your unbelief’). In verse 4 the earliest manuscripts have Peter say ‘I will make three shelters’, while the Byzantine text has ‘let us make’, followed by the King James Version. In verse 22 the best manuscripts read that they were gathering together (systrephomenōn) in Galilee, while the Byzantine text reads that they were staying (anastrephomenōn), the King James Version's ‘while they abode in Galilee’. In verse 9 manuscripts vary between two verbs for rising, with no difference in meaning. Translation differences matter in verse 15, where the King James Version's ‘he is lunatick’ renders the Greek word for moonstruck, and modern versions give ‘has seizures’ (BSB) or ‘is an epileptic’ (RSV). The promise of Elijah, Malachi 4:5-6 in English Bibles, is Malachi 3:23-24 in the Hebrew Bible.

teach.big: The Father reveals Jesus as his beloved Son whose glory is real but reached through suffering, so his disciples must listen to him, trust him with even the smallest faith, and follow his example of freedom exercised in humility.

outline.t: Jesus' glory is his own, the Law and the Prophets give way to him, and the Father's command for every disciple is ‘Listen to Him’.
Glory and suffering belong together: the forerunner was rejected, and the Son of Man will be too, so the vision makes sense only after Easter.
The Son of the mountain comes down to the suffering, and his authority is shown in compassion for a desperate father and his son.
Disciples fail when their trust is too small, yet the smallest faith in the right God is enough for what seems impossible.
Jesus names his death and resurrection again, and grief is the right first response to the cost of the cross.
The Son is free, yet he lays aside his rights to avoid needless offense and pays for another; Christian freedom serves love.

teach.pitfalls:
The transfiguration is often preached as a lesson about ‘mountaintop experiences’, with the moral that we cannot live on spiritual highs. There is truth in the contrast with the valley, but the passage is about who Jesus is, not about managing religious emotions, and the three disciples were terrified, not elated. Peter's offer of shelters is sometimes mocked as foolish; the text says only that the Father interrupted him to point to his Son, and his wish to honor the moment was natural.

Verse 20 is the text most often misused. It has been taken to mean that anyone with enough faith can obtain healing, wealth, or success, and that failure proves a lack of faith. Jesus says the opposite of that measurement: mustard-seed faith is tiny, and its power lies in God, not in the believer's intensity. The saying should never be used to blame the sick for their illness. The healing should not be taught as proof that seizures are demonic; Matthew describes this boy, and the Gospels elsewhere list the demonized and those with seizures separately (4:24). Finally, the coin in the fish should not become a promise of miraculous provision for anyone who needs money, or a curiosity to explain away; it is a teaching about the Son's freedom and his care not to give offense.
teach.pastoral: This chapter will press on families who live with epilepsy or with a child's serious illness. The father's plea, ‘Lord, have mercy on my son’, gives them words, and Jesus' response is compassion, not a diagnosis of anyone's sin. Teachers should say plainly that epilepsy is a medical condition to be treated, that it is not a sign of demonic possession, and that no one's illness proves weak faith. Those who have been told by a church that they were not healed because they did not believe enough need to hear that Jesus blamed the disciples' little faith, not the father's, and still healed the boy. Verse 23, where the disciples are deeply grieved, gives permission for sorrow in the face of death. And for believers who feel their faith is only a flicker, the mustard seed is good news.

hard.q: Was the boy suffering from epilepsy or from a demon, and how should modern readers take the Gospels' accounts of possession?
hard.a:
The objection is strong. The father's description (seizures, falling into fire and water) matches what medicine calls epilepsy, and Matthew uses the ancient word ‘moonstruck’. Ancient physicians had already rejected supernatural explanations: the Hippocratic treatise On the Sacred Disease, from the fifth century BC, argued that the condition has natural causes, and the historian of medicine Owsei Temkin (The Falling Sickness, 1945) traced how belief in demonic causes of epilepsy persisted for centuries and brought great suffering on people with the condition. Critics, and many Christians, conclude that the Gospels describe a medical condition in the categories of their time, and that reading this story literally has contributed to the stigma of people with seizures.

Christian responses differ. Some read possession here as the ancient explanation for a condition now understood medically, and see in Jesus' act compassion and healing expressed in the terms his hearers used. Others, such as Graham Twelftree (Jesus the Exorcist, 1993), argue that exorcism was a central and historically secure part of Jesus' ministry, that the Gospels bear witness to real evil powers, and that such powers may act through physical symptoms; they note that the Gospels themselves distinguish ordinary illness from possession, listing the demonized and those having seizures separately (4:24), and that Matthew elsewhere reports healings of illness with no mention of demons. Many Christians hold both convictions together: epilepsy is a medical condition that should never in itself be attributed to demons, and Jesus did confront and defeat real powers of evil. On any of these readings, the passage gives no ground for treating people with epilepsy or mental illness as possessed, and the Gospel's own emphasis falls on Jesus' compassion, his authority over whatever held the boy, and the disciples' need for faith.

hard.q: Did a fish really carry a coin, or is the story a folk tale attached to Jesus?
hard.a:
The skeptical case begins with the parallels. Herodotus tells how the tyrant Polycrates of Samos threw his precious ring into the sea and found it days later inside a fish served at his table (Histories 3.41-42), and the Babylonian Talmud tells of Joseph who honored the Sabbath and found a precious stone inside a fish he bought for the Sabbath meal (b. Shabbat 119a). David Friedrich Strauss (The Life of Jesus, 1835) treated the coin in the fish as a legend, and many critical scholars see a folk motif of treasure in a fish joined to a saying of Jesus about the sons being free. They add that the story is found only in Matthew, that it is a miracle for Jesus' own convenience of a kind he refused elsewhere (4:3-4), and that Matthew never narrates it actually happening.

Responses take several forms. Interpreters from John Chrysostom (Homily 58 on Matthew) onward have read it as a real miracle of foreknowledge and provision, noting that it is not done to spare Jesus hardship but to avoid offending others and to provide for Peter as well. Others observe that the story's weight lies in the dialogue, not the fish: the unit is a pronouncement story whose point is the principle in verses 25 and 26, and the command in verse 27 matters for what it shows about Jesus' attitude, whatever one concludes about the catch. Some note that fish in the lake do take bright objects and that barbels there are caught with a baited hook, as Mendel Nun observed, though the point of the story is not what fish can swallow but what Jesus knew. Commentators such as W. D. Davies and Dale Allison, who collect the folk parallels, also point out the differences: in the Polycrates tale the return of the ring is an omen of ruin, and in the Talmud the jewel rewards piety, while here the coin serves a Son who pays a debt he does not owe. As with other miracles, the verdict depends in part on prior convictions about whether God acts in this way; the chapter itself asks readers to attend chiefly to the Son's freedom and humility.

observe: What details does Matthew give about Jesus' appearance, and what exactly does the voice from the cloud say?
What reason does Jesus give for the disciples' failure to heal the boy, and what does he promise about mustard-seed faith?
What question does Jesus ask Peter about the kings of the earth, and what reason does he give for paying the tax anyway?
interpret: Why do you think Moses and Elijah appear and then disappear, leaving ‘no one except Jesus’? What does the command to listen to him add to the Father's words at the baptism?
Why might Jesus forbid the disciples to speak of the vision until after the resurrection?
How does Jesus' payment of a tax he did not owe connect with his teaching and his death elsewhere in Matthew?
apply: What voices compete with Jesus' for your attention, and what would it mean for you to listen to him this week?
Where does your faith feel as small as a mustard seed? How does it change things to know that its power lies in God and not in its size?
Is there a right you could set aside, as Jesus did with the tax, so as not to put a needless obstacle in someone else's way?
